claims: A filibuster is a U.S. Senate procedural tactic used by the minority party to delay or block a vote on legislation by extending debate.
Invoking cloture requires a three-fifths majority (60 votes) to force a final vote on legislation subject to filibuster.
A filibuster can be bypassed for certain budget or nomination matters.
The silent filibuster is currently the most common form.
In the silent filibuster, a senator threatens to filibuster, leading leadership to shelve the bill rather than waste time.
The silent filibuster effectively requires 60 votes to pass most legislation.
The talking filibuster historically involved a senator or group of senators taking the floor to speak continuously, preventing a vote.
To break a filibuster, the Senate must vote for cloture.
The U.S. Senate (.gov) website notes that the filibuster originated from the Senate's tradition of unlimited debate and the lack of a mechanism to force a vote.
Senate Rule XXII was adopted in 1917.
Rule XXII allowed for cloture (initially two-thirds majority, now 60 votes) to end debate.
A Brady United article says the filibuster was used to block anti-lynching legislation in the early 20th century.
Strom Thurmond held the previous record for a filibuster speech against the Civil Rights Act of 1957.
According to the Brennan Center for Justice, Senator Cory Booker broke the filibuster record in April 2025 by speaking for over 25 hours.

The Brennan Center for Justice explains that the primary purpose of the filibuster is to allow the minority party to block, amend, or delay legislation they strongly oppose, protecting their rights and forcing negotiation
